subject: math
description: Students recognize that a measure of center (mean or median) summarizes an entire numerical data set with a single typical value, while a measure of variation (range, interquartile range, or mean absolute deviation) summarizes how spread out the values are with a single number. They distinguish which kind of summary a question calls for, compute center and spread for small data sets, and interpret what each number tells you about the data. This is a conceptual standard: the emphasis is on what center and spread mean and when each is the right description, not yet on building displays (that is 6.SP.B).
subSkills: Classify a statistic as a measure of center or a measure of variation
Compute the mean as the sum of values divided by the count, $\bar{x}=\frac{\sum x}{n}$
Find the median of an ordered data set (middle value, or mean of the two middle values when $n$ is even)
Find the interquartile range $\text{IQR}=Q_3-Q_1$ from an ordered list
Compute mean absolute deviation (MAD) as the mean of the absolute distances from the mean
Interpret a single summary number in context (what a center or a spread tells you about the values)
Decide whether a question is asking for a typical value (center) or for how much values differ (variation)

problemArchetypes.name: Classify the statistic
problemArchetypes.example: Which of these summarizes the spread of a data set rather than its center: mean, median, or interquartile range? Answer: interquartile range.

problemArchetypes.name: Compute a measure of center
problemArchetypes.example: Find the mean of $4, 7, 7, 10, 12$. Sum is $40$, count is $5$, so $\bar{x}=\frac{40}{5}=8$.

problemArchetypes.name: Compute the median
problemArchetypes.example: Find the median of $3, 9, 5, 12, 7, 7$. Ordered: $3, 5, 7, 7, 9, 12$; the two middle values are $7$ and $7$, so the median is $\frac{7+7}{2}=7$.

problemArchetypes.name: Compute mean absolute deviation
problemArchetypes.example: For $5, 7, 9$ the mean is $7$; deviations are $2, 0, 2$, so $\text{MAD}=\frac{2+0+2}{3}=\frac{4}{3}$.

problemArchetypes.name: Choose center vs. variation in context
problemArchetypes.example: A coach wants one number for the typical height of players and one number for how much heights differ. Which measures should she use? A center (mean or median) for typical height, and a measure of variation (range, IQR, or MAD) for how heights differ.

problemArchetypes.name: Interpret a single summary number
problemArchetypes.example: Two classes both have a mean quiz score of $80$, but class A has range $6$ and class B has range $40$. What does the difference in range tell you? Class B's scores vary far more even though the typical score is the same.

Easy.description: Single-step recall or one computation on a small, already-ordered data set. The student either classifies a named statistic as center vs. variation, or computes one measure where the arithmetic is clean (whole-number mean, odd count so the median is a listed value, range as a subtraction).
constraints: Data set has 3 to 6 values, listed in increasing order
Mean comes out to a whole number; median is an odd-count middle value
Only one statistic is requested, and it is named explicitly (e.g. 'find the range')
No MAD or IQR; only mean, median, or range
Classification items ask only 'is this a center or a variation measure?'

Medium.description: Requires an ordering step or a two-part computation. Median of an even-count set (average the two middle values), mean that is a non-whole fraction, range or IQR that requires first sorting an unordered list, or computing both a center and a spread for the same data set.
constraints: Data may be given unordered and must be sorted first
Even count so the median is the mean of two middle values
Mean may be a fraction or decimal
IQR requires locating $Q_1$ and $Q_3$, or a simple MAD on 3 to 5 values
May ask for two statistics (one center, one spread) on the same set

Hard.description: Multi-step reasoning or interpretation. Compute MAD fully, compare two data sets by center and by spread and explain what differs, work backward (find a missing value given the mean), or read a context and decide which kind of measure answers the question and justify why.
constraints: MAD requiring mean, all absolute deviations, then their mean
Compare two data sets and interpret why equal centers can have different spreads
Reverse problems: given the mean and all but one value, find the missing value
Context items that require choosing center vs. variation and justifying the choice in words

difficultyRubric.tierSplit: This standard uses a single ramped worksheet (worksheet.single, 15 items, Easy to Hard). It is a conceptual standard with modest computation, so it does not warrant a tier1/tier2 split. If it were split, tier1 would cover classification plus mean/median/range (Easy to Medium) and tier2 would cover IQR, MAD, comparison, and interpretation (Medium to Hard).

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses a measure of center with a measure of variation
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Calls the range a measure of center, or names the mean when asked for a measure of how the values vary

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student finds the median without ordering the data first
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Reports the physically-middle value of the unordered list, e.g. for $3, 9, 5, 12, 7$ answers $5$ (the third value as written) instead of the true median $7$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student uses the wrong count when computing the mean (divides by a value other than $n$)
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Divides the correct sum by the largest value or by the number of distinct values instead of $n$, e.g. $\frac{40}{4}=10$ instead of $\frac{40}{5}=8$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student treats range as max plus min instead of max minus min
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For values from $2$ to $14$ reports $14+2=16$ instead of $14-2=12$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student computes MAD without taking absolute values, so the deviations cancel to zero
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Reports $\text{MAD}=0$ because the signed deviations from the mean always sum to $0$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses IQR with range, subtracting min from max instead of $Q_1$ from $Q_3$
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Reports $Q_3-Q_1$ replaced by $\text{max}-\text{min}$, giving the range value when the IQR is asked for

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student assumes equal centers mean identical data sets
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Claims two sets with the same mean must have the same spread, ignoring that range or MAD can differ
